history.period: 15th-16th century; begun under Devaraya II (1422-1446), expanded under Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529); left unfinished after the Battle of Talikota (1565)
history.summary: The Vittala Temple is the most celebrated monument of Hampi, dedicated to Vitthala, a form of Vishnu. Construction began under Devaraya II and the complex was lavishly embellished under Krishnadevaraya, then abandoned unfinished after the 1565 Battle of Talikota and the sack of Hampi by the Deccan sultanates. It is famous for the monolithic stone chariot (a Garuda shrine imitating a processional temple car) and the hall of musical granite pillars that ring when struck. Unlike most South Indian temples it is no longer an active place of worship; it is an ASI-protected archaeological monument and the centerpiece of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Group of Monuments at Hampi' (inscribed 1986). Legend says the deity found the temple too grand and returned to his humble home. NOTE: Hampi lies in Vijayanagara district (created 2021; earlier Ballari district), Karnataka - coordinates from map geocoding (approx. 15.34N, 76.48E).

name: Vittala Temple
town_description: Hampi, on the southern banks of the Tungabhadra River, was the imperial capital of the Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1565). Its boulder-strewn landscape is scattered with palaces, temples, and markets that now form the UNESCO World Heritage 'Group of Monuments at Hampi'. It is both a major archaeological site and a living pilgrimage town centered on the active Virupaksha Temple.
